title: India's Fertiliser Ministry Wants to Double Its Subsidy Budget. The Fiscal Year Is Three Months Old.
excerpt: With global fertiliser prices surging and El Niño threatening the monsoon, New Delhi is already scrambling to contain a cascading food security crisis that could touch every Indian household.
body:
India's Department of Fertilisers has asked the Finance Ministry to double its budgeted subsidy allocation for the current fiscal year — and the financial year is barely three months old. The request, first reported by Reuters and confirmed by a senior government official, signals the depth of the strain that the Iran war has placed on India's fiscal machinery and its food supply chain.

The government had originally earmarked its standard annual outlay for fertiliser subsidies in the Union Budget presented in February. But the prolonged blockade of the Strait of Hormuz — through which a fifth of the world's crude oil and liquefied natural gas normally passes — has sent global fertiliser prices spiralling upward. Urea, diammonium phosphate (DAP), and muriate of potash (MOP) have all surged, with India importing significant quantities of each.

**The numbers are staggering.** New Delhi has already disbursed ₹1.2 trillion ($12.6 billion) in direct support to oil marketing companies to keep petrol and diesel pump prices frozen for the first 78 days of the war. The fertiliser subsidy demand now threatens to add a comparable fiscal burden, squeezing the government's ability to maintain its ambitious capital expenditure programme without blowing through deficit targets.

## Two Crises Converging

What makes the situation especially dangerous is that India's fertiliser crisis is not arriving alone. It is colliding with an El Niño weather pattern that the India Meteorological Department says has already pushed the south-west monsoon to an 18 per cent deficit since its late arrival on June 4 — three days behind schedule.

Sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific crossed the drought-bearing El Niño threshold of +0.80°C as of June 7, according to Australia's Bureau of Meteorology. All forecasting models point to continued warming through the year. A severe El Niño typically brings dry weather across South and Southeast Asia, cutting crop yields and pushing food prices higher.

India's sugar industry is already showing strain. Acreage has stagnated in key growing regions of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, carry-forward inventory is thinning, and the government recently aborted a planned sugar export window. Industry experts warn that the tightening buffer will force the Centre to prioritise domestic retail availability at the expense of ethanol blending targets.

## What This Means for the Rupee and the Household Budget

The fertiliser subsidy is not an abstract line item on a balance sheet. It directly determines what Indian farmers pay for inputs, which in turn shapes the cost of wheat, rice, pulses, and vegetables on every kitchen table — from Lucknow to London, from Chennai to Chicago.

"India is set for a series of supply shocks," said Michael Langham, emerging markets economist at Aberdeen Investments. "Apart from pressure on oil prices, the country also faces supply disruptions to fertiliser as a result of the Iran war, which will impact key crops like wheat when farmers are already bracing for an El Niño."

Economists at multiple institutions have flagged the overlapping nature of these shocks. The RBI held the repo rate unchanged at 5.25 per cent at its June meeting, citing the amplified risks to inflation and growth from the conflict's duration and spillover effects. Governor Sanjay Malhotra acknowledged that the "rare Goldilocks phase" he had celebrated at the end of 2025 had been upended.

## The Diaspora Angle

For the estimated 32 million Indians living abroad, the fertiliser crisis has immediate implications. Food price inflation in India directly affects the families many NRIs support through remittances. Higher domestic costs erode the purchasing power of money sent home — even as remittances hit a record $43.5 billion in Q4 FY26.

At the same time, the government's decision not to cut back capital expenditure, despite the unplanned spending, suggests New Delhi is betting that domestic consumption can absorb the shocks. But if the monsoon fails and food prices spike, that bet could unravel, dragging India's GDP growth below the 6 per cent mark that has been its floor for most of the past decade.

The war may be in the Middle East. The drought may be in the Pacific. But the bill is arriving in Indian homes — and the government is still figuring out how to pay it.
